name: Psalms
v: Listen, my people, to what I'm teaching. Lean in close to the words from my mouth.
I'm opening my mouth in story and saying — I'm cracking open riddles buried since the beginning,
the things we've heard, the things we know, the things our fathers told us.
We won't hide it from their children. We'll tell the next generation the praises of the LORD, his power, the wonders he worked.
He set a testimony in Jacob, planted a Torah in Israel — commanded our fathers to teach it to their children,
so the next generation would know, even the children not yet born, so they could rise and tell their own children —
so they would put their hope in God and not forget what he's done, but keep his commands.
So they wouldn't be like their fathers — a generation stubborn and defiant, hearts that wouldn't hold steady, spirits that wouldn't stay faithful to God.
The men of Ephraim, armed, carrying bows — they turned and ran on the day of battle.
They didn't keep God's covenant. They refused to walk in his Torah.
They forgot what he'd done — the wonders he'd shown them.
In front of their fathers he worked the impossible, in Egypt, in the fields of Zoan.
He split the sea and walked them through. He stacked the waters up like walls.
He led them by a cloud in the day, by a fire's glow all through the night.
He cracked open rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink as deep as the deep itself.
He pulled streams out of stone — water cascading down like rivers.
But still they kept on sinning against him — defying the Most High in the desert.
They tested God in their hearts, demanding the food they were craving.
They spoke against God: "Can God set a table out here in the wilderness?
Sure, he struck the rock and water gushed and torrents flooded — but can he hand us bread too? Can he get meat for his people?"
The LORD heard. Fury erupted. Fire blazed against Jacob. Wrath rose against Israel —
because they didn't believe in God. They didn't trust his power to save.
So he commanded the skies above. He threw open the doors of heaven.
He rained manna down on them to eat — gave them grain straight from heaven.
Mortals ate the bread of angels. He sent them food until they were stuffed.
He stirred up the east wind in the heavens, drove the south wind by his strength.
He rained meat on them like dust, birds with wings like the sand of the sea.
He dropped them right in the middle of camp, all around their tents.
They ate and gorged themselves — he gave them exactly what they wanted.
But before they'd even swallowed their craving — while the food was still in their mouths —
the wrath of God rose up against them. He cut down their strongest men. He felled the choice young men of Israel.
And still — after all this — they kept sinning. They didn't believe his wonders.
So he ended their days in futility, their years in sudden terror.
When he killed them, they'd come looking for him — turn back, search for God in earnest.
They'd remember God was their rock, the Most High God their redeemer.
But it was just lips. They flattered him with their mouths. They lied to him with their tongues.
Their hearts weren't fixed on him. They weren't faithful to his covenant.
But he — full of mercy — covered over their guilt and didn't destroy them. Again and again he held back his anger. He didn't unleash all his wrath.
He remembered they were flesh — a breath that blows past and doesn't come back.
How many times they defied him in the wilderness — wounded him out there in the wasteland.
Over and over they tested God. They provoked the Holy One of Israel.
They didn't remember his hand — the day he ransomed them from the enemy,
when he set his signs against Egypt, his wonders in the fields of Zoan.
He turned their rivers to blood — they couldn't drink from their own streams.
He sent swarms of flies that devoured them, frogs that ruined them.
He handed their crops to the locust, their labor to the swarm.
He killed their vines with hail, their sycamores with frost.
He gave their cattle over to the hail, their livestock to lightning bolts.
He unleashed on them the heat of his anger — fury, indignation, calamity — a delegation of destroying angels.
He cleared a path for his anger. He didn't spare them from death. He handed their lives over to plague.
He struck down every firstborn in Egypt — the first fruits of strength in the tents of Ham.
But his own people he led out like sheep, guided them through the wilderness like a flock.
He led them safely — they weren't afraid — and the sea swallowed their enemies.
He brought them to his holy border, to this mountain his right hand had taken.
He drove out nations before them, measured them out an inheritance with a line, settled the tribes of Israel in the tents of the conquered.
But they tested God Most High and defied him. They didn't keep his statutes.
They turned back — traitors like their fathers — twisted like a warped bow.
They provoked him with their high places. They made him jealous with their carved gods.
God heard. Fury. He utterly rejected Israel.
He walked out of his tent at Shiloh — the dwelling he'd pitched among humans.
He let his strength go into captivity, his glory into the hand of the enemy.
He handed his people over to the sword — was furious with his own inheritance.
Fire consumed their young men. Their young women had no wedding songs.
Their priests fell by the sword. Their widows couldn't even weep.
Then the Lord woke up — like a man waking, like a warrior sobering from wine.
He drove his enemies back, broken, and shamed them forever.
He rejected the tent of Joseph. He didn't choose the tribe of Ephraim.
He chose the tribe of Judah — Mount Zion, the one he loved.
He built his sanctuary like the heights of heaven, like the earth he founded forever.
He chose David, his servant — took him from the sheep pens,
brought him in from following the nursing ewes to shepherd Jacob his people, Israel his inheritance.
And David shepherded them with a heart of integrity. With skillful hands, he led them.

com.d:
# Psalm 78: The God Who Never Forgets

This great psalm is a meditation on covenant faithfulness—God's relentless refusal to abandon His people despite their chronic unfaithfulness, and a solemn call to pass that story forward to the next generation.

The psalmist begins by insisting that this is not merely old history to be archived and forgotten; it is living testimony meant to be told and retold. The repeated failures of Israel—their murmuring in the wilderness, their forgotten miraculous deliverances, their worship of idols—are recounted not to shame the past but to awaken present faithfulness. Each generation seems to arrive at the same crossroads where their ancestors stumbled, forgetting what God has done. Yet God, remarkably, does not forget. He bears with them through exodus, wilderness, conquest, and kingdom, sometimes in judgment but always with the intention of restoration.

What strikes us most deeply is that God's forgiveness is not forgetfulness. The Lord remembers that His people are "flesh, a wind that passes and does not come again." This is not indifference but tenderness. God knows the weakness of His people and yet commits Himself to them anyway. He chooses a shepherd, David, and builds a house that will last forever. The pattern is unmistakable: human failure, divine patience, covenant renewal.

For us today, this psalm becomes a humbling mirror. We inherit the same tendency toward spiritual amnesia—forgetting yesterday's provision when today brings uncertainty, building idols out of comfort or success, wandering from the God who has proven faithful. Yet we also inherit the promise. The God who bore with ancient Israel remains the God who bears with us. He has not changed His nature; He does not grow weary of calling us back.

The real weight of this psalm lands in its implicit command: tell the next generation. Do not hide your failures or God's grace. Make known His deeds, His strength, His wondrous works. This is how faith lives.

What stories of God's faithfulness in your own life are you called to share with those coming after you?
com.s:
Psalm 78 stands as one of the most extensive historical psalms in the Psalter, attributed to Asaph, the Levitical musician appointed by David to lead worship in the tabernacle. This magnificent composition of seventy-two verses functions as a didactic recitation of Israel's salvation history, employing the genre designation *maskil* in its superscription, indicating its instructional purpose for the covenant community. The psalm's setting likely reflects the early monarchic period, possibly composed to legitimate the Davidic dynasty and the choice of Zion following the rejection of the northern sanctuary at Shiloh.

The opening verses establish the pedagogical framework through the term *mashal* (מָשָׁל), traditionally rendered "parable" but more accurately understood as a wisdom teaching or instructive comparison drawn from ancestral tradition. This terminology connects the psalm to the broader wisdom tradition while emphasizing the intergenerational transmission of covenantal memory. The complementary term *chidot* (חִידוֹת), meaning "riddles" or "dark sayings," suggests that the recounted history contains deeper theological significance requiring careful reflection—the events themselves constitute divine revelation demanding interpretation.

The psalm's literary architecture traces a cyclical pattern of divine grace, human rebellion, divine judgment, and renewed mercy, covering the span from the Egyptian exodus through the establishment of Davidic kingship. Particularly significant is the repeated use of *marah* (מָרָה), describing Israel's rebellion as bitter provocation, which occurs at critical junctures emphasizing the persistent unfaithfulness despite witnessed miracles. The theological tension between divine *chesed* (חֶסֶד), God's steadfast covenant loyalty, and human *shikchah*, the forgetfulness of God's mighty acts, drives the narrative forward.

Scholars debate whether the psalm's selective historical memory—emphasizing Ephraim's failure while exalting Judah—reflects northern-southern political tensions or serves purely theological purposes regarding divine election. The climactic movement from Shiloh's rejection to Zion's choice represents not merely geographical relocation but theological reconstitution of sacred space. Within canonical context, Psalm 78 occupies a central position in Book III of the Psalter, contributing to the collection's meditation on exile, covenant, and divine faithfulness despite national catastrophe, offering subsequent generations both warning and hope rooted in remembered redemption.
com.p:
This magnificent historical psalm, composed by Asaph during the early monarchic period around 1000-950 BC, stands approximately one thousand years before Christ's incarnation. It surveys Israel's story from the Exodus through David's enthronement, placing it firmly within the Kingdom phase of redemption history—after God delivered His people from bondage and gave them the Law, but before the tragic division and eventual exile that would follow Solomon's reign.

Asaph opens with a solemn declaration of intent: to speak in parables and dark sayings from of old, a phrase the Holy Spirit later reveals as messianic when Matthew applies it to Christ's teaching ministry. Here the typological pattern emerges immediately—the psalmist who teaches Israel through veiled wisdom prefigures the greater Prophet who would open His mouth in parables, revealing things hidden since the foundation of the world. The wisdom teacher of old shadows the Wisdom of God incarnate.

The psalm rehearses Israel's stubborn rebellion despite God's magnificent deliverances: the plagues upon Egypt, the parting of the sea, the pillar of cloud and fire, water from the rock, and manna from heaven. Each of these mighty acts carries prophetic weight. The smitten rock from which living water flowed typifies Christ crucified, from whose side flowed blood and water—the true spiritual drink for God's pilgrim people. The bread from heaven, which the fathers ate yet died, anticipates the true Bread of Life who descended from the Father, of which whoever eats shall never perish.

Yet the recurring theme of Israel's faithlessness despite such wonders constitutes a sober eschatological warning. They tested God repeatedly in the wilderness; they forgot His works and demanded satisfaction for their cravings. Divine judgment followed divine patience. The generation that witnessed Sinai's fire perished in unbelief—a pattern the author of Hebrews would later invoke to warn the new covenant community against hardening their hearts.

The psalm culminates in God's sovereign election of Judah over Ephraim, Zion over Shiloh, and David as the shepherd-king over Israel. This is no mere political transition but prophetic preparation: from David's loins would come the eternal Shepherd-King who tends His flock with upright heart and skillful hands. The church now lives under that Davidic reign, warned by Israel's failures, nourished by heavenly bread, and awaiting the day when rebellion ceases and God dwells with His people forever.
